speechtext:
I desire, with the consent of the Committee, to proceed with the consideration of a resolution, which I shall introduce, relative to the tariff. The House will recollect that in the Budget speech I gave notice of two resolutions, one affecting special taxation which the Government proposed and the other relating to certain tariff increases under the proposed War Revenue Act. It will be more convenient for me, if the committee is agreeable, to proceed first with the consideration of the resolution which I shall present dealing with the increases in the tariff. We are considering certain modifications in the phraseology, and slightly in the substance, of the resolutions relating to special taxation. I have not at present- but expect to have later in the afternoon-copies of the resolution as modified.
Now, with regard to the resolution relating to the tariff changes, I desire to say that there are certain modifications which I have to propose, one new item and a small number of additions to the list of exemptions. At the request of the Government of Newfoundland we propose to place upon the free list wild edible berries. I

have to propose also certain additions to tl>e list of exemptions as follows:	At the request of the Government of the sister colony of Jamiaea, I propose that bananas shall he exempted from the increase in tariff under the War Revenue Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is au
excellent move.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend knows that excellent moves are characteristic of me. Why should he express surprise at one?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yet I'do. But better late than never. That is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
These berries are known as partridge berries, and grow on the rocks of Newfoundland.
I have added to the list of exemptions, silk in the gum or spun silk imported to be used in the manufacture of woven labels. Woven labels manufactured of silk come under the operation of schedule C of the French treaty, and consequently are not subject to the increased duties of 71 and 5 per cent proposed in the Budget. Silk in the gum or ispun silk imported to be used in the manufacture of woven labels, therefore, will also be exempted from the rates in question.
I am placing manuscripts also upon the free list, at the request of the Customs Department, who istate that it is almost impossible to fix a valuation upon which the rates of duty could be imposed.
There are two other important items: Coffee and coffee extracts. Hon. gentlemen will recall that in the August 'session we increased the duty upon coffee and upon its products, including coffee extract. From a careful consideration of the matter -since bringing down the Budget, I have reached the conclusion that to add a special war tax to the 'special tax imposed at the August session upon coffee would probably have a not inconsiderable effect upon the trade, especially in view of the fact that tea has been left upon the free list. Tea is largely used in eastern Canada and coffee in western Canada; both, of course, are largely used throughout the Dominion.
Then there is platinum. Platinum is about three times as valuable as gold. It is used for laboratory and other purposes, and the tax of 71 and 5 per cent would be exceedingly heavy if placed upon it. We
propose, therefore, to include platinum in the list of exemptions.
I come now to the item of fertilizers. Since the Budget was brought down, requests have reached us from the Agriculture Department, in connection with its campaign for increased production throughout Canada, to consider favourably the placing of fertilizers- in the list of exemptions. Similar requests have been made by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House. The amount involved is not large; apart from	this, it is, of course,
a pleasure	to the 'Government to
further in any possible way the propaganda of the Agricultural Department which has for its object the increase of production throughout Canada. I propose, therefore, that items 662 and 663, which cover manufactured and unmanufactured fertilizers, be included in the list of exemptions, and in addition to that we include also acid phosphate of lime, sulphate of ammonia, nitrate of soda, muriate and sulphate of potash, when imported to be used for fertilizing purposes. I think that these three items cover all manufactured and unmanufactured articles known as fertilizers or the raw material which enters into their manufacture.
Will there be remissions of duties paid since February 12?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This provision will relate back to the date of my Budget speech, from which date the duties were collected.
Do we understand that duties paid under the original provision will be refunded? I have had many letters on the subject from persons who have paid these duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There will be a refund,
because this provision will relate back to February 12, the date when the duties become operative.
Should there not be some provision to cover that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it is amply covered in the resolution which I have prepared, and which I shall present in due course.
There is one other item which was drawn to my attention-I speak from memory, but am satisfied that I am correct-by the Minister of Agriculture for the province of Ontario. It is that of cotton seed cake and cotton seed cake meal used for feeding purposes. We propose to include that in the list of exemptions.
That is what is commonly known as cotton seed meal, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is my understanding of it. Their technical designations are as I have given them.
They were so designated in the last tariff, but this product is called cotton seed meal by the general public.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I believe that is correct. Another item which we propose to exempt is No. 45, milk foods used by hospitals and for the feeding of infants. When I speak of exemptions, the House will understand that I mean exemptions from the operation of this war tax of 7J and 5 per cent.
The war tax upon spirits is a matter of some importance. This duty was formerly specific; under the proposals of the recent Budget importations of spirits become subject to the 7} and 5 per cent rates. I pointed out the other day that we were imposing a duty of 5 per cent and 7J per cent on imported spirits and that the distiller of spirits of domestic manufacture would have an increased cost in his manufacture by reason of the fact that his coal and his corn and machinery and other materials would be subject to a special taxation of 7J per cent and 5 per cent. Since the Budget speech it has been brought to my attention that the duties under the War Revenue Act would apply to the fair selling value of spirits at the place from which they were imported and that included in that fair selling value is the excise duty levied by the foreign government. We propose that, so far as the imposition of these customs taxes is concerned, these excise duties shall be disregarded in estimating the value of goods for the purpose of our amendment to the customs tariff of 1907. I hope I have made myself clear. Under the Customs Act at present, spirits are imported into Canada and an ad valorem duty is imposed, that ad valorem duty would take effect upon the fair selling value of the spirits, say in Great Britain or in Holland or in any other country, including in that, the excise duties imposed by the Governments of those countries. I propose that that should be disregarded and that the 7J per cent or the 5 per cent, as the case may be, should be imposed upon the selling value, disregarding the excise duty which I have mentioned.
The excise imposed in the country of origin would be a part of the price there, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Precisely.
You exclude the foreign excise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly. The reason we are doing that is that it is important that if we are to be fair in the imposition of these taxes, while we should see that the home producer, that is to say, the distiller, has a tax imposed, so to speak, to protect him- I am not using that in the fiscal sense-as against the added cost of his production, the cost of his production would be compared with the cost of the production abroad, and the foreign excise should therefore be disregarded. We think that the proposal we are now making will be fair to these importers of spirits and fair also to the distiller here.
Under the new arrangement, is the distiller of Canada not given more protection than he had before the Budget was brought down?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Than what I am now proposing? No, I do not think so. As the Budget was brought down the proposals would have imposed a tax of 7J per cent or 5 per cent, as the case might be, on the price of the spirits in the country of origin from which they were imported. Included in that price, in fact the major part of that price, is the excise charged by the Government in the country of origin. As I brought down my proposals, the 7J per cent and the 5 per cent would be levied upon, let us say, $2 as the price of a certain amount of liquor, including foreign excise; whereas now I am excluding foreign excise and the 7i per cent will operate only on a very much less amount of the price.
It will be on the selling price less the excise of the country of origin?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Will it be on a flat declaration of that kind? Will your regulations say that the customs duty will be imposed upon the selling price in the country of origin less the excise duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The proviso is:
Provided also that excise duties shall be disregarded in estimating the market value of goods for the purpose of this amendment to the Customs Tariff Act of 1907.
Would not the excise be a part of the selling price? Is not the excise tax paid by the foreign producer in the country of origin part and parcel of the selling price?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No doubt, that is, if the
goods are for home consumption.
How can you separate them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The invoice value of goods exported in bond will not include the excise duties.
You propose in the first place in exacting the duties to ascertain the selling price and then specifically deduct the excise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The invoice value is always the price less the excise duties.

I do not think the minister understood the question of the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Law.) The question was: Will the changes which my hon. friend now' proposes still leave a greater protection to the Canadian producer of spirits than he had before the hon. gentleman's Budget speech on February 12?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think so for this reason, that the distiller will have to pay the same rates, the 7.) per cent or the 5 per cent, upon his raw materials and upon his machinery and not only that, but it is by no means clear that the price will at once rise to the level of the existing price plus the 7) per cent or the 5 per cent.

And then on the other side of the account my 'hon. friend has pointed out what the distiller will pay. On the other side of the account he will have the protection of 7) per cent on
4 p.m. the cost of the article in the country of production, less the excise duty.
In that case it would be the importer who gets the advantage and not the distiller.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the importer brings it in the duty is less. No doubt my hon. friend has that in mind. What I am doing is to cut dowm the amount of duty which will be paid upon the importation on spirits.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Tha* is an improvement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am glad that my right hon. friend again says that is an improvement. Before I get through my right hon. friend will probably be wholly converted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend allow' me? When he brought down these resolutions I drew his attention to the fact that the distiller had an advantage of
7.J per cent upon the foreign article coming into competition with his goods, w'hich in-73
eludes in the price to the consumer the excise duty; and the excise duty upon spirits is very high in all countries. A gallon of spirits will, as a rule, cost in the neighbourhood of $3, the cost of production being about 50 cents per gallon, and the excise about $2.50 per gallon. Therefore, the distiller w'ould have 7) per cent upon the $3, the selling price in the country of origin. If my hon. friend drops the excise, and calculates the duty upon the cost of production without the excise, the distiller would still have a protection of 7| per cent on 50 cents, not on $3-a still large protection. Against that you say that the distiller in this country would have to pay 7J per cent upon his corn and upon his coal; and the point of the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Law) was whether you are yet giving a large protection to the distiller. It is not possible for me to go into that fully, because I do not know the value of the coal or the corn that goes into the production of one gallon of spirits. But I think there is still protection in favour of the distiller.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the amount will be almost negligible; it will be small at all events. The large factor pointed out by my right hon. friend is the excise. Shortly after I brought down the Budget I was waited upon by the representatives of the spirit trade, who pointed out that previously the duties had been specific, and that these proposals would give an undue or disproportionate advantage to the distillers. Upon consideration it appeared to me that their complaint was well founded; and this appears to me to be the solution of the difficulty, for I think it will be substantially fair to the spirit trade, and substantially fair also to the distiller. In dealing with this question we must not forget that labour and capital are cheaper in European countries than here; and I need not go into the question of overhead charges. Therefore, having regard to the fact that the distiller has to pay the duty upon his coal, upon his corn, and upon his machinery, and having regard also to the fact that he has higher operating charges than abroad, I think that any advantage he might get from this tariff would be inconsequential.

The minister has mentioned Britain and Holland. Could he give any idea as to the percentage of the fair selling price of a gallon of whisky? I mean the proportion between the cost of production and the excise paid in the for-



eign country? Would it be 50 per cent each, or 25 per cent and 75 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I might say that the price of liquor per gallon is about 40 to 50 cents in bond, but the excise duties vary in different countries.

Take Britain or Holland,
the two countries mentioned by the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The question of excise does not come in at all in the proposals of the Minister of Finance.
If you take it out, and we could easily reckon the cost of production know the cost of a gallon of whisky, we in a foreign country-

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Foreign countries sell their liquor as we do, in bond. In England it would be about 40 to 50 cents a gallon, and they do not have to pay the excise duty in that country.
That answers my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: There is no excise duty upon liquor that is exported from those foreign countries. It is necessary to state that it is the price in bond, for the reason that in our old tariff it is specifically mentioned as so much per gallon. The question of price is not so important, on account of it being mentioned in the original tariff as per gallon. But in this case it is necessary to have it stated in the tariff that it is the price of liquor as sold in bond.

I wanted to find out what the liquor really cost in the country of production, and I think the Minister of Customs has answeTgd my question. He says 40 to 50 cents. We can easily argue from those figures. If a duty of 5 or 7| per cent is applied, we can easily find out to what extent the home producer of liquors is protected.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I made an inquiry in consequence of what my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) asked a moment ago, and the information afforded has been practically given, by both my hon. friend the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Finance. But perhaps the answer may not have been clearly understood. The difficulty has arisen from the fact that for the most part the duties imposed upon liquors, both by way of excise and by way of customs, have been specific duties, which of course are very high. Now, under the Tariff Act, the value upon which

the duty must be imposed is the fair selling price in the country of exportation, but in the case of liquor the fair selling price in the country of origin is very largely composed of excise duties. Perhaps 75 per cent is composed of excise duties if the liquor is sold in that country. But in other countries, as well as in this country, when liquor is sold for export, the excise duty is not paid. Therefore, if the proposals as first brought down were to be interpreted in that way, and apparently the customs authorities think they would be so interpreted, the result would be that a tax would be imposed upon an amount three-fourths or four-fifths of which was not paid by the importer. Do I make myself clear?
Yes, I understand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: For that reason, in order to get the fair selling value, within the meaning of the Act, it is proposed to disregard that portion of the supposed selling value which is not really paid by the importer and which is represented by an excise tax upon the goods exported from the country of origin and imported into this country. So that it comes down practically to this: The 5 or 7J per cent duty is to be paid upon the price which the importer actually pays for the liquor that he brings into this country.
Which would be 40 or 50 cents a gallon according to the Minister of Customs.

Instead of having a mixed tariff, would it not have been better to have imposed an additional specific duty, which would be equivalent to the 7J per cent on the selling price in the country of origin?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed that the
Customs Department can administer the tariff in respect of the commodities we have been speaking of at the ad valorem rates. For uniformity, with, I think, one exception, we have determined upon the 7J. and 5 per cent general horizontal raise in the tariff, as I stated in the Budget. I gave consideration to the question drawn to my attention by the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), and discussed the matter with my tariff officers, and they discussed it with the Customs Department. They see no difficulty in administering the tariff under the ad valorem rates, which are in addition to the specific rates.

Has the minister considered the advisability of levying the per

cent on the fair selling price in the country of production and putting on sufficient excise in Canada to equalize the matter, adjusting it so that you get the revenue, and the home manufacturers get no more protection? In my judgment, that is the proper course to pursue. My hon. friend may say there is such a thing as taxing an article beyond the point of producing revenue. As far as I am concerned, you can tax whisky just as high as you want to, and if we do not get the revenue out of it we will not have the stuff in the country. I think it would have been better if the minister had added on the excise in Canada and balanced up the price to the importer after he had levied the 7$ per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The rates of duty of 5 per cent and 71 per cent on the liquor that will now be imported will be estimated on a value of say about 40 cents per gallon, the export price from the exporting country. If the duty is 5 per cent it will be two cents per gallon, and if it is 7J per cent it will be three cents per gallon, in addition to the present customs tax of three dollars per gallon.
Suppose you had left out the tariff proposals of a month ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Wait till I answer this question. The manufacturer of liquor in this country pays 7J per cent additional on his corn. Sixty cents per bushel is a fair average price for corn. That would be about five cents per bushel, in addition to which he pays duty on his coal. The duty that would be paid on the quantity of liquor produced from a bushel of corn would about balance up the duty that would be imposed on liquor coming from a foreign country. So far as the liquor manufacturers in Canada are concerned, I cannot see that they are getting any advantage, such as has been suggested by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

This is not a question
entirely between the importer of liquor and the distiller. Is it not of some interest to the people? They are paying a tax upon practically everything that they eat or wear, and they are interested in the rates of duty that may be imposed. Under the Budget as brought down there was to be a duty of 7J per cent from countries to which the general tariff applies, and of 5 per cent from countries enjoying the British preference, and these rates were to apply to all spirits imported into Canada. I understand that 73J
by the present proposals it is intended to reduce the value of these imported spirits for duty purposes by 75 per cent. It is stated that the excise amounts to 75 percent of the value, and there/ore, instead of spirits worth $1,000,000 paying a duty upon $1,000,000, as they would have to pay under the Budget as brought down, by this change they will only pay a duty upon $250,000. Is that fair? My hon. friend has sought to impose taxes all round; he says tney are going to bear equally upon all the people-and that he is going to raise so much revenue. Then, when he is brought face to-face with the fact, as pointed out to him by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, that he ought to have increased the excise duty as against the distiller; so kindly disposed is he towards the distiller that he says:	I will not do that, but I
will make it all right to tne importer by reducing his valuation to the extent of 75 per cent:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is against the distiller.
No, it is in favour of the importer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is against the distiller.
It is against the distiller, but it could have been made equitable as between the distiller and the importer by raising the excise duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) answered his own question and also the objection of the hon. member from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). He stated that there is a point beyond which, if you carry your taxation you defeat your own ends.
Can the hon. gentleman tell me why that happens?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend knows well why it happens.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have no conclusive
evidence, but the opinion of the experts of the Customs Department and of my department is that with the excise that we imposed last August upon liquors and tobacco we reached the maximum in so far as excise is concerned, and that if we increase

beyond that point instead of getting a greater revenue we will get less revenue. That is the answer to my hon. friend.
We have had six months' experience; what is the result?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend can analyse the result as well as I can. My hon. friend knows that many factors have entered into the consideration of that question during the past few months, such, for instance, as the dislocation of trade and commerce. I am not going over the ground that has been traversed so frequently during the late debate, but my view is that we cannot increase the excise without defeating our purpose, which is to obtain more revenue.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There would be a less consumption of liquor then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Possibly so.
That would not be an unmixed evil.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not discussing that question now; we are discussing a revenue Bill. Probably my hon. friend, if we were speaking of it from another standpoint, would find that I was not less desirous of restricting the consumption of liquor in Canada than he is. But we are not now dealing with that question; we are dealing with the question of revenue. Our starting point is that it is not advisable to increase the excise in the interest of obtaining revenue. That being so, if we had allowed the 74 per cent and the 5 per cent to apply to the fair selling price-and as my hon. friend the Minister of Customs has pointed out, goods are sold abroad in bond and regard should be had also, as required by the Customs Act, to the excise , of the foreign country-the effect would be to give the distillers altogether too great an advantage, and that is what my hon. friend had in his mind when he called my attention to it. That is what my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition had in his mind, and that is what was drawn to my attention some time ago by the spirits trade. What we are seeking to do is to get the maximum of revenue and to so deal with our revenue proposals that neither the distiller on the one hand nor the spirit importer on the other will have an undue advantage; in other words, to get the maximum of revenue with fairness and justice to all concerned.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The argument of my hon. friend (Mr. White) is not an

answer at all to the objection of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). The hon. gentleman says that we cannot increase the excise because we would defeat the object of the Bill, which is to obtain revenue. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance thinks that he will get revenue if he adds 74 per cent to the customs duties. If the trade can support 7) per cent of an increase in the customs tariff on liquor it could support also an excise duty. The two things always go together.
The Minister of Finance says he cannot afford to reduce his revenue, because if he puts more excise on he will defeat the purpose he has in mind. If you put the customs duty at 74 per cent you expect you will have the same quantity of liquors coming in and that you will get the increased revenue, but in the matter of spirituous liquors excise duty and customs duty always go together. It is the intention of the legislation that there should be no protection and that the whole revenue should go into the treasury. If there is more duty on the liquor that comes from abroad, there will be less production here, and if there is less coming from abroad there will be more production in Canada. In order that there should be no protection to the distiller all governments have wisely provided that there should be a customs duty equalled by an excise duty; in other words, that the duty paid on every drop of liquor which is consumed in this country shall go into the treasury.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There has been an
excise duty corresponding to the customs duty, but there has been additional customs duty as well. My point is that the distiller must pay upon his raw materials 74 per cent. The 74 per cent will apply, not to the selling price abroad, having regard to the excise contained in it, but upon the selling price abroad without regard to the excise. My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) states that we would have got a certain amount of revenue from the liquor that would come in if we imposed a 74 per cent or a 5 per cent increase upon the selling price of the liquor abroad, including the excise. My answer to that is simple: if I did not amend as I am now amending, the liquor would not come into the country. The duty would be too high in competition with the home-manufactured article, and therefore I would not get as much revenue as I now get.

If the same quantity
of liquor was used as before, whatever was

lost from customs would be gained by excise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is begging the question. I am proceeding upon the ground that you cannot increase the excise by 71 per cent without defeating your purpose.
Can you defeat your purpose unless there is a lesser use of intoxicating liquors ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a different question and we are not arguing that. Some day it may be necessary to argue the question as to whether it would be desirable to limit the importation and consumption of liquor, but the question before us now is the question of getting revenue, and at present we are considering a revenue measure. If I did not make this amendment I would not get the same revenue. My hon. friend says the same amount of liquor will be consumed, and that we can make up for the decrease by putting excise on the home-made article. We have considered that and we have come to the conclusion that we could not put the 71 per cent on the home-made article without defeating our purpose to raise additional revenue.

The Minister of Finance will admit that the only way he could defeat his purpose by making the excise duty too high would be that he would not get as much money from excise. The same quantity of liquor would be imported as long as people continue to use intoxicating liquor, and what he would lose in excise he would gain in customs. On the other hand, if he left the customs duty as he proposed, then anything he lost in customs he would gain in excise. Is not this the fact: That the Minister of Finance has really been tender towards the distiller. There is no class of people in this country who have made more money out of their business than the distillers of Canada; there is no wealthier class in the country than they, and there is no class which requires less consideration, so far as excise duties are concerned. It does seem to me that what the Finance Minister ought to have done was to have increased the excise duty, if he wanted to equalize the obligations as between the importers and the distillers. Instead of doing that, he proposes by a scratch of the pen to take off 75 per cent from the tariff duty which has to be paid by the importer. That is what the Minister of Finance purposes doing. The effect of what the hon. gentleman says
is, that if he leaves the import duty as proposed and he increases the excise duty, he will make the cost of liquor in this country greater. Everybody admits that the result of this tariff will be to make the cost of clothing, the cost of foodstuffs, the cost of all the necessaries of life greater by the extent not only of the duty imposed but also by reason of the extra price which will be charged by the manufacturers on the home product. Suppose the people of this country who use intoxicating liquors have to pay a little more than they do now, and suppose they have to bear their share rf the burdens which all the people of this country are called upon to bear by reason of this so-called war tax, would there be any great evil in that? I do not believe that the use of intoxicating liquors will be affected one iota by the raising of the excise duty or the increase of the import duties. If they want to drink liquor at the club, in the hotel, in the bar-room, in their private houses, they will drink liquor notwithstanding that a few cents more per gallon are added to the cost. Of course, the Minister of Finance knows that I do not agree with his tariff at all and that I believe it is all wrong, but instead of making a reduction and seeking to lessen the burdens on those who drink intoxicating liquors, he ought to have left the import duties as they were, and if he wanted to equalize matters as between the distiller and the importers he could have raised the excise duty to a reasonable amount. Then if as a result people did not buy as much liquor which was distilled in Canada, there would be so much more imported, and whatever the Government might lose in excise duty it would gain in customs duty.

Do I understand the
hon. member to lay down the principle that the raising of the tariff rates will not decrease the consumption of liquor?
My view is that the raising of the tariff rates as proposed will not materially reduce the consumption of liquor-.

Do I understand the Minister of Finance to argue that the additional duties imposed upon the raw materials of the distillers are the equivalent of the additional excise, and for that reason no substantial excise duties are imposed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not desire my hon. friend to understand me as saying that. We are dealing with a 7J per cent ad valorem duty. The question is raised as to whether

it is effective and if so to what extent additional protection is given to the distiller. The distiller has to pay upon his corn, and upon his coal, and upon his machinery and his packages, the war revenue tax on the basis of 7J per cent or 5 per cent. As a set-off to that, and also for the purpose of obtaining revenue, we are imposing the 7j per cent and the 5 per cent upon the selling price. It is necessary I should insert this proviso because if I did not, under the provisions of existing legislation, the customs officials would have regard to the foreign excise tax.
I think we understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Very good, then; my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) took the view that we are depriving ourselves of revenue by making this change, and he also put forward the assertion that we were tender to the distiller. My hon. friend knows as well as 1 do that in making this change, instead of being favourable to the distiller it is distinctly unfavourable to the distiller as compared with the proposals in the Budget, because the product of the distillery here is in competition with the spirits imposed by the import trade. Therefore, what I am doing, instead of being favourable to the distiller, is decidedly unfavourable to him. I am not doing it to be unfavourable to the distiller, but to do simple justice as between the distiller and the importer. My hon. friend says, why not raise the excise 7J per cent and let the 7J per cent as it is remain on imports? My answer is that in August last we imposed very substantial additional taxation upon spirits and I have been advised by the experts of the Excise Department and of the Customs Department that we have raised it up to about the maximum point, and that if we carry the duty beyond a certain extent there will be smuggling and illicit manufacture, and there might also be a diminution of consumption which would reduce the revenue. We are not dealing with the question of advisability or non-advisability of diminishing consumption-or, at least I am not- the only question is as to additional revenue. It seems clear to me that we shall not deprive ourselves of additional revenue by reason of imposing the additional 71 per cent upon the selling price disregarding the foreign excise duty, because, as the proposals were brought down, on account of our not having inserted the proviso I now propose to insert, the importations would be greatly diminished, and there-

fore our revenues would fall off although the rate would apply upon a higher value than will now be the case. Therefore, the answer is in regard to increasing excise I am advised that I should defeat my purpose. As to the duty on imports, in the first place I should receive less revenue under the proposal of the Budget than I shall now obtain; and secondly, unless my proposals were amended the distiller would have an unjust advantage. What I propose to do is to put our proposal upon a just and equitable basis so that I shall get, as I judge it, the maximum of revenue, and at the same time hold the scales even as between -the import trade and the distiller, and not give the distiller a disproportionate advantage.

I cannot speak for other
provinces, but I know that in the province of Quebec the consumption of liquor must have fallen off materially during the past year or two. In thp lower part of Quebec between Levis and Campbellton there is not a single licensed hotel.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There has
not been for many years.

Not for many years. In Montreal 70 licenses were cancelled by the License Commissioners, the Government of Quebec allowing compensation to those who sold out. The liquor business in Montreal has fallen off very materially. A wholesale liquor dealer told me a few days ago that whereas an ordinary saloon in Montreal would sell $400 or $500 worth of whisky in one week, the sales have fallen off to $125 or $150 a week. I read this morning that one of the famous night cafes in Montreal which have caused	so	much discussion, was
recently sold out, the whole	outfit
being knocked down under the auctioneer's hammer. But, as the minister says, we are not discussing this from the moral point of view, but from the point of view of revenue. The great objection to the kind of liquor sold in Quebec is that it is often greatly adulterated. I remember that a few years ago-the hon. Minister of Finance was not here then-the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) gave us an elaborate explanation of the manufacture in Toronto of Scotch whisky, liquor of a very inferior quality, that never saw the Highlands of Scotland-nor the Lowlands either. It is an infraction of the law to sell as Scotch whisky that which is not the genuine article? And is there, under excise regulations or otherwise, any control by the

Dominion Government over the selling of poisonous drugs under the name of whisky, such as are sold in many bars to the poorer classes of people?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I am unable to answer my hon. friend with any authority. I understand that, in the case of whisky, if the word " Scotch " should be taken to apply to the quality of the liquor and not to the place of origin there would be some redress. But my opinion is not worthy of weight because I have not specially looked into the matter. I think that the hon. member (Mr. C. Marcil) does not dissent from the views I have expressed because if he is interested in seeing that there shall be quality in the liquors, then it is obvious that there should not be a disproportionate or inequitable advantage to the home manufacturer. In other words there should be a stimulus to competition as between the home manufacture and the imported article.

I thank the minister for his explanation, but I fear I did not make plain the point I wished to bring out. I wished to know if there is any system of inspection over the manufacture of liquor in Canada. I often see newspaper advertisements of whisky in which appear some such words as "Inspected by Government officials." Is that really the case with all the liquor manufactured in Canada, or not?
Mr. W'HITE: In a sense, I think it is, because the manufacturer is required to keep the product a certain time. But I do not believe-though I should be glad to be corrected if I am wrong-that the Dominion carries on inspection as to quality. It is quite possible that the provinces do, as they issue licenses for the retail and wholesale sale of liquor.

I do not wish to insist on the point, but the minister will see the importance to the labouring and poorer classes, if they must have liquor, that it should not be of a poisonous character. Some of the drugs sold to the working classes as liquor are nothing less than poison.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have explained the modifications which I have proposed, and I desire to move this resolution, which is the resolution of which I gave notice in my Budget speech, modified as I stated in my opening remarks to-day.

Would not the order be to pass the original resolution through committee and then propose the
other? Or is the minister only presenting this as an amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I took the opportunity of consulting the Clerk of the House on the subject. He stated that I had given notice of the resolution, but had not moved it, and therefore I could move this resolution in committee, which, as I have stated, embodies the modifications I have made in the resolution of which I gave notice in the Budget speech. I believe the procedure is regular. If there is any doubt about it, I could move to have the resolution of which I gave notice amended by this.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think the regular procedure would be, if there is to be a departure from the original notice, to give the notice again. But we will not insist on that. *

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I inquired as to that. If 1 were proposing to increase the burden of the tax, I should give notice, but what I am doing is exempting, and that, I understand, can be done in committee without notice. But I should be glad to oblige my right hon. friend in any way, and, if he desires, to allow this to stand as a notice of motion. But there are so few amendments made that I suggest we might proceed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Before proceeding, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance upon his having yielded, even if only after some four weeks' discussion, to the protests made by this side of the House with reference to some very onerous and some very unwise impositions proposed in hjs Budget speech. I want to refer especially to the taxes on fertilizers. As to that, I do sincerely congratulate the Finance Minister and the Government for having even at this late date acquired wisdom as 'to what it is proper to do in the interests of the farmers of Canada. My hon. friend has said that representations were made to the Government by members on both sides of the House in favour of exempting fertilizers. Surely my hon. friend is mistaken as to that. The hon. member for Assiniboia protested against the duties on fertilizers, showing that it was proposed to increase the duties upon fertilizers 'coming from Great Britain by 100 per cent, and upon fertilizers coming from the United States and other countries under the general tariff by 75 per cent. He pointed out that this was a marked instance in which a preference was given not to Great Britain, but to the United States. I myself called attention to this onerous burden proposed

to be placed upon the farmers, and quoted from letters *which I had received protesting against the imposition of such a tax. But hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House justified this proposed burden upon the farmer. The hon. member for North Essex justified it, and other hon. gentlemen, equally eloquent, equally forcible in their argument and equally influential, justified it. My hon. friend said it was a small thing to be divided among 800,000 farmers, as if every farmer in Canada were going to use a part of the fertilizer imported and pay part of the aggregate duty. This is but another evidence of the fact that whatever proposal my hon. friend and his colleagues make to the House, hon. gentlemen behind him are ready to back it up, to support it, to justify it. However, for hon. gentlemen to go even this short distance, by reversing their proposals, in encouraging the farmers to increase their production, is worth the three or four weeks discussion which we have had in this House. I have taken a very humble part in bringing light and understanding to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, but even for the little that I have been able to accomplish I am very thankful indeed. My hon. friend will realize that other hon. members on this side of the House have led him into the proper path.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The taxes that we proposed are for the purpose of meeting the situation caused by the war. Our intention was to make the increase fairly general in its operation. We made a number of exceptions. I am quite certain that the farmers of the country would be willing to pay the tax in question for the purpose that we had in view in imposing it. The times are not normal; in norma] times we should not have brought down these proposals. It appeared to me from the discussion that took place that certain sections of the country are possibly more immediately interested in this tax than other sections are; certainly, having regard to the size of the country and the extent of the farming community, the tax as a whole would have been a small one. But, as I stated, it has been represented to me that the placing of fertilizers in the list of exemptions might tend to facilitate the propaganda of the Department of Agriculture, which has for its object the very laudable and, indeed, patriotic purpose of increasing production in Canada. As I say, the proposed tax is small, but even if

it had been larger, in view of the requests made, as I have said, by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, I need not say that it would have been a pleasure to me to place it in the list of exemptions. I could argue justification for the tax and for all the proposals that we have brought down, having regard to the very extraordinary situation which we have been compelled to meet. However, I am glad to receive congratulations, if they are in order. We have placed the tariff rates upon fertilizers precisely where they were before. As everybody seems to be happy-
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend not happy?
No, you have not gone far enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have gone farther than my hon. friend's tariff went.
Eliminate the tariff on fertilizers; then you will be doing something.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend was a long time there before I was here; I do not know that he made very much progress in that respect. What we have done is, I think, very fair, and will meet the requests that have been received from various parts of the country through the Agricultural Department.

I should like to draw the attention of the Finance Minister and the Government to the matter of gravel, which was formerly on the free list, but now to be subject to a duty of 7] per cent. The hon. minister rather smiles at that suggestion

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, no.
Mr. PARDEE-But I can assure him that it is a very burning question in our part of the country. We have great difficulty in getting this material for the purpose of manufacturing concrete for foundations, etc. It is one of the crying necessities of our farming community. I think that what I say in this respect will be borne'out by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) and by the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Wilcox). Not very long ago a large deputation waited upon the Government, and I think that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Public Works were among the gentlemen who received that deputation. They laid

before the Government their request that gravel should be brought in and distributed by the Government free of charge. At that time I said that although I was not wholly in accord with that plan, I thought that everything should be done by the Government that could be done in order to enable the farmers to get this commodity in the easiest possible way. At the present time practically one company has the'whole concession along the St. Clair and Detroit rivers, in so far as the Canadian side is concerned. They have secured this concession under license from the Dominion Government and the Provincial Government of Ontario, and no person else is allowed to go there and take away gravel.
What company has the concession to which my hon. friend refers?

I think it is the Cadwell Sand and Gravel Company of Windsor. As a result, those persons who desire to deal in that commodity have to go to the American side of the river, bring the gravel into Canada, and pay a duty of 7{ per cent upon it. Having regard to the peculiar need of the community-although perhaps not so much to that peculiar need as to the peculiar way in which this commodity has to be obtained-and to the fact that the revenue the Government would receive from this source would not be very great, it would be a great help to the farming community if they were enabled to obtain this commodity at as little cost as possible. It might be well for the minister and the Government to take into their very careful consideration the restoration of the articles under that tariff item to the free list. I can assure the minister that such an action would be greatly appreciated and that although it may look like a small thing it is a question of very burning importance in our part of the country, whatever it may be elsewhere. The revenue derived from the imposition of this tax of course will be trifling and will be more than counterbalanced by the resulting benefit to the farmers.

In view of the fact that
the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Pardee) has made some reference to the Windsor Sand and Gravel Company, as I have some knowledge of the business in which they are engaged, it may be wise for me to make a few remarks. Complaints have been made to me upon former occasions. While the hon. member for St. John was Minister of Public Works, that is before the change of
Government, three large sand bars in the St. Clair river required constant dredging in the interests of navigation, the expenditure on them running from $25,000 to $35,000 a year. The Windsor Sand and Gravel Company applied for permission to dredge the bars, and entered into an agreement to furnish 2, 3, 4 or 5 dredges if need be to keep that channel open to navigation. The company put in an equipment costing them over $60,000. From that day to this they have kept the channel open, free of cost to the country. The company have no exclusive rights under their agreement, they have simply a permit and the Government are free to grant similar rights to any other company or individual.
I am not making a plea against the company, I am asking that this protective duty be removed.

I understood my hon.
friend to say that the company had the exclusive right.
Yes, so it has.
That is not the information given me by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley). I have seen the lease and my recollection is that it did not state that they had an exclusive right.
Clear of that altogether, should the duty be imposed?

As a farmer, and I believe that I obtain the same view as other farmers, I have always felt that we want to pay our honest share of the increased taxes of this country. I do not believe in this handing out of something to the farmers of this country as a kind of a sop in which there was little or nothing with the object of creating a little sentiment to get a few votes.
I am glad my hon. friend takes that view. His farmers will be glad.

I never heard of gravel
being imported in my part of the country. The gravel is all got along the Canadian side. All around lake Erie, lake Ontario and the Detroit river, the gravel is got on the Canadian side. In any case, very little sand or gravel taken from the lakes is used by the farmer, to discuss it in this way is only hair splitting, because the farmers in my part of the country get their gravel and sand in the southern portions of the country, where there are many good pits, some of them 30 and 40 feet deep.
The hon. gentleman referred to a contract that I had to do with as Minister of Public Works. I am not quite sure that I rememDer the locality; but is it not in the international river.
Yes.

And does not the company dredge from both sides of the boundary line? I know they take gravel over to the United States and it goes in free of duty, but I thought that in some cases they brought it from the United States to this side.

My hon. friend is right. The Canadian side is gravelly. The action of the stream carries the lighter parts, the sand, to the American side, and when the company desire sand, as I understand it, they have to get it from the American side because there is no sand on the Canadian side, only the heavier portions, the gravel.
With respect to the duty on fertilizer, which my hon. friend says I commended, I think the Minister of Finance spoke of some one being unhappy, and the right hon. leader of the Opposition said very quietly, Wilcox.
I want to assure my hon. friend that I am perfectly happy. My remarks with regard to this subject were more to put my hon. friend right on the question of squid, because he mistakenly argued that squid was a fertilizer. That was the introduction of the fertilizer topic.
A very adequate justification, very happy.
My hon. friend knows that he was mistaken; he admitted he was mistaken, apd he spoke of using it as a spray for trees.

Did not the hon. gentleman tell the House that the total duty on fertilizers was only $4,600, and when a correction was made did he not say it was a mere bagatelle on the farmers of the country, anyway?

My hon. friend must not put words into my mouth. He is always good natured, and I shall be good natured, too. But I am not going to stand for my hon! friend's putting words into my mouth that I did not use. I explained the matter fully, and my hon. friend said that I had given him a complete answer when I had said that one figure had been left out. I said that the duty amounted to $46,000, and that the census returns showed that there were 800,000 farmers in this country, and TMr. Wilcox.]
that therefore the duty averaged five and three-quarter cents apiece. We do not use this fertilizer extensively in our part of the country. It is used, however, by a number of farmers who are engaged in intensive farming. For instance, there is a Mr. Ellis who has five acres under glass in Leamington. I was present at his plant in the month of April, when he picked a ton of tomatoes for-which he received 25 cents a pound. On the whole winter's operations he cleared $13,000. Now, that man uses a good deal of fertilizer, and he is just as able and as willing to pay the duty as any other man in this country. I was very much surprised yesterday when the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) told us how much fertilizer was used in his county. I have absolutely no objection to the amendment suggested by the Minister of Finance. I only wished to explain what I had said in regard to what this war tax would bring, and what it would average to the farmers of this country. I believe that the farmers realize the death and misery on the battlefields of Europe, and the issues that are involved in this great conflict, and I believe they are willing to pay their share of the duties because we are living happy and free, so to speak.

I am
very glad that the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Wilcox) is not going to object to the putting of fertilizer materials on the free list. He states that fertilizer is not very extensively used in his part of the country. I represent the adjoining county, and I wish to join with the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and other members in expressing my gratification that fertilizer materials are to be put on the free list. I am sure that the constituents whom I have the honour to represent will appreciate it very much. There are men in the county of Kent who use as much as four or five tons of fertilizer a year, and these men are classed among the most successful farmers in the province of Ontario. The duty originally proposed would have been quite an item to them, and for that reason I take this opportunity of thanking the Finance Minister for having made this change.
I am sure it will be of considerable benefit to the people I have the privilege to represent. Might I at the same time ask the Minister of Finance to take into his consideration the question of putting on the free list the machinery that is used for putting fertilizer on the ground for the different crops. Many kinds of implements are used foi; this purpose in connection

with planting beans, corn, tobacco, and sugar beet, and only a very small percentage of this machinery is made in Canada; so that if the minister granted this request it would, at the worst, be depriving only a few of our labourers of work, and it would be of great assistance to our farmers who grow such varied crops. I am sure they would greatly appreciate it. N-1 should also line to say that I am heartily in accord wim what the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) has said in connection with gravel and sand. The hon. member for North Essex said in substance that the farmers in his section of the country would not consider it very serious if this tax was kept on. In my section of the country large quantities of sand and gravel are used. If I remember correctly, when the deputation met the Minister of Public Works and other ministers some time ago, it was the hon. member for East nambton (Mr. Armstrong) who made the greatest protest against what, if carried out, would have assisted the farmers of south-western Ontario in the way of putting up barns and improving sidewalks in uie villages and towns. I believe that on that occasion Mr. Cadwell represented the concern winch has the exclusive right of getting gravel and sand from me auierent rivers that have been referred to. So that you see he was looking after his own nnancial interests, while other gentlemen were endeavouring to find ways and means whereby the gravel and sand could be distributed through the different counties in south-western Ontario at as low a price as possible. I cannot agree with the hon. member for North Essex that the Cadwell Company should be allowed this exclusive privilege. I think other firms should be given an opportunity of competing. If the plants required in this business are so expensive that other firms cannot see their way clear to going into the business, then I agree with the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) that no further protection should be given to this concern by putting a duty of 7i per cent on the material which is needed so badly in south-western Ontario. That is the position I take. I appeal to the Minister of Finance to give this matter his most serious consideration, and not to allow this firm any longer to compel the farmers of this country and the citizens of the different villages to pay just what they see fit for the gravel and sand that is so necessary for tne improvement of the country generally.
Mr. J. E. ARMSTRONG (East Lambton); I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) in bringing this matter before the House. It is one of very great interest to the people living in the western peninsula, who are compelled to make use of these materials for building purposes and for road-making. If they wish to bring in building material to the Western peninsula they have to go something like a hundred miles to get it; in fact, it is almost impossible for the people in the western district to get building material for roads or bridges or for what is required around the farms, unless they get it from the Cadwell Stone and Gravel Company. It is true that a year or two ago a deputation came to Ottawa with the object of persuading the Government to cancel the contract with the Cadwell Stone' and Gravel Company, which was entered into under the administration of the ex-Minister of Public Works.

May I correct the hon. gentleman? As I understand it, the Department of Public Works had the right only to give a license to dredge or reclaim sand in navigable waters. The power to give an exclusive right to take that sand from the bed of rivers lay with the Ontario Government, and it. was from the Ontario Government that they got their exclusive right. The Department of Public Works, during the time of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), only went so far as to give them a license to dredge in navigable waters.

I understood from Mr. Cadwell, president of the Cadwell Sand and Gravel Company, that he was quite willing that any other dredge should go in there and take its share of the material. I am confident that I was right when I asked this Government to cancel that contract in the public interest and allow any person to go there, take sand or gravel and distribute it to the farmers and to the cities and towns at the lowest possible cost. If this Government had been allowed to carry out their good roads policy I feel confident that a portion of the money to be devoted to that purpose could have been invested to the very best possible advantage in Government dredges employed for the purpose of recovering and distributing sand and gravel to people generally in the western peninsula at practically cost. That

was the proposition that I placed before the Government, but unfortunately they had not the means to carry it out. They did investigate it, however, and when the time comes that we have sufficient money set aside for the purposes of good roads, there is no doubt that a portion of it should be applied to the dredging of sand and gravel from the mouth of the St. Clair river. Tens of thousands of yards come down and block the channel. The sand and gravel that comes down to the mouth of the St. Clair river comes from the Canadian shore. A portion of the sand, no doubt, goes to the American shore. I understand from the Minister of Public Works that at present any dredge is at liberty to go on the Canadian part of the river and dredge whatever sand and gravel it pleases, but if, as these hon. gentlemen say, the Cadwell Sand and Gravel Company have an exclusive right, then I would urge upon t'he Governmnt in the public interest to discontinue that contract and allow any one to go and take sand and gravel and use it for the purposes suggested by the hon. members for West Lambton and West Kent.

As I understand the contract, any person can go there at the present time and obtain a portion of the material. How many dredges other than those used by the Cadwell Sand and Gravel Company are dredging the material at the mouth of the river and disposing of it to farmers and citizens in general? I would like to ask the hon. member for West Lambton and the hon. member for West Kent to be good enough to name any companies which are likely to go to the United States side of the river, obtain this material, pay duty on it, and bring it into Canada. It seems almost absurd to expect that they would do anything of the kind.

The objection I have to this exclusive right lies in the expensive machinery that it takes to operate this business. No person is going to put thousands of dollars into a dredging outfit to supply sand and gravel, but if we put a duty of per cent .against American concerns, thus preventing them from coming in here with their sand and gravel, it means that we give an exclusive right to these people and they will take advantage of this item

and extract from the users of sand and gravel just so much more money.
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to give me the names of one or two American firms which supply sand or gravel in Canadian towns or cities along the border ?
That is a very specious question. May I answer that question by asking him to answer my question as to whether he is in favour of the 7i per cent duty ?
If the hon. gentleman cannot name an American firm that has been delivering sand or gravel at any time on the Canadian side, then surely their argument falls to the ground.
I do not agree with the hon. gentleman that the Cadwell Sand and Gravel Company have the exclusive right.
If they have not ?
If they have not, what is the use of it ?
Then, would the hon. gentleman be in favour of putting on a 7J per cent duty ?
I am not here to be cross-questioned.
Very well; let it go at that.

The hon. gentlemen opposite have been unable to say that any sand or gravel has been brought from the American side of the river to the Canadian side. If none has been ,brought in during past years, and if the contract does not hold good, why would you expect that any would be brought in in the future ?

If the hon. Minister of Finance cannot remove that 7J per cent duty, would he give us the assurance that if the Cadwell Sand and Gravel Company raises the price to the consumer he will then remove the duty ?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid that we are losing sight of the purpose of this tax. This tax is general, and I think it inadvisable to make any exceptions unless they are clearly in the public interest or it is manifestly unfair that the parties paying it should contribute under the circumstances to the war expenditure of this Dominion. Therefore, I say, that the question of whether there is an exclusive privilege or not has no bearing on the matter.
I have laid the full proposals before the House, and they are very general in character. There are a number of exceptions to them, some of which I have mentioned this afternoon. There is no gentleman in this House to whose representation I would be disposed to pay more favourable attention than the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee). It is not a matter of dealing with this question abruptly, but I must maintain the principle that the object of this legislation is to obtain revenue, which but for the war it would not be necessary for us to obtain. It is admitted that the quantity of this sand required is comparatively small, and that the taxation upon it will consequently be small. I do not see my way at present-although I would be very glad to look into the matter-to make an exception in this case, because if I make an exception in this case and not upon principle, then I do not see how I can very well refrain from making exceptions in other cases. If the matter were large and if it were vital I would be disposed to give it more consideration, but the amount involved is small and it is extremely undesirable that we should widen the list of exceptions. We are going to need these revenues' to meet the financial condition of the Dominion which, as I maintain, has been occasioned in large measures by the war.

I would ask the hon.
member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) and the hon. member for West Kent (Mr. McCoig) why the municipalities bordering on the lake that have not applied for shore rights under the provisions of the Beaches and Shores Act passed by the Ontario Government about four years ago. Any municipality can send its township engineer to lay out certain sections along the shore, and after that plan has been confirmed by the Ontario Railway and Municipal Board, all the farmers within the municipality have the right to take sand from the district outlined in the plan. That was done in my township of Rochester, and the farmers are obtaining sand at fifteen cents per load.
The riparian owner owns the foreshore; the Government has no right to it.
The water lots are under the jurisdiction of the Government.
Yes, but the foreshore is owned by the riparian owner.

No.
Mr. PARDEE
Yes.

It is owned to the high
water mark.
Yes.
From the high water mark to a point out about six feet is the water lot which is under the jurisdiction of the province.
Quite so; but a man cannot take sand from under the water.
The sand 1 have reference to drifts in along the lake.

That belongs to the
riparian owner.

But if the farmers are
authorized by the Ontario Railway and Municipal Board to get sand the law gives them the authority to do so and the price is stipulated by an order of the board.

During the last two weeks
some very harsh and unjust language has been hurled from the Government side of the House against the members of the Opposition, but now the Minister of Finance has seen fit to rebate the duty on fertilizers and on cotton-seed oil, and of that I am very glad. I believe that if the Opposition has accomplished nothing else by what the minister has called obstruction, we will

certainly have the good will of the farmers of the country for having the tariff on these items changed. I am very glad that I can claim some small credit for that, because in the few remarks I made the other day I advocated that the duty should not be raised on fertilizers or on cotton-seed oil. The question of the duty on spirituous liquors will come up again and I do not wish to say anything further about it at the present time. However, I am sorry the minister has seen fit to at all rebate the tax on liquors. I should have been quite willing to have supported a very much heavier tax on liquors had he proposed it.

I want to present the question of this tax on fertilizers in a little different form from that in which it has been before presented. I do so because in my own constituency probably one-third of all the fertilizers imported into Canada are consumed. The quantity imported does not nearly represent the total consumption, because there are large quantities of these commercial fertilizers manufactured in the maritime provinces, and I am satisfied that our farmers purchase as much of the home product as they do of the imported. I believe I am well within the mark when I say that the fertilizers used by the people in my constituency cost about $400,000 per annum. We are paying on that a ten per cent tax. It is true, as the Minister of Finance says, that this duty existed when the Liberals were in power, but that does not alter the matter, and the tax is there just the same. The consumption and the use of these fertilizers has greatly increased in recent years, and I am satisfied that until 1911, $50,000 or $75,000 would represent the value of fertilizers used in my constituency. The business has gone on, perhaps faster than it should, but be that as it may it means that the farmers of my constituency are paying a tax of $40,000 yearly for fertilizers, and if they do not pay it to the customs house they pay it to the man who compounds the mixture. To show that there is no protection necessary I need only point out that the manufacturer or the compounder of commercial fertilizers in the maritime provinces sells as much of his commodity in the state of Maine as he does in New Brunswick. The last day I was at home a gentleman came to my office and asked me if there was not some way by which he could have the thing arranged so that he could buy a certain grade of fertilizer in the state of Maine

which was manufactured in New Brunswick, and bring it back to Canada without paying duty. He took the ground that it being a Canadian product he should have the right to bring it in from the United States free of duty, because as he said:	here is an
article manufactured not a hundred miles from where I live, then exported to the United States, and if I could go across to the United States and buy it and bring it back I could buy it for four dollars a ton cheaper than I could in Canada. I feel diffident about asking the Minister of Finance to depart from the principle which he feels like following, but I would point out that in this campaign of patriotism and production nothing is more important than the entire remission of the duty on fertilizers.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: What is it worth per ton?

It is worth from $40 to $42, and I fear we will have to pay a little more for it this year and get a much poorer grade as we cannot obtain our potashes
from Germany.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is it sold on analysis?

Yes, under the Fertilizers
Act passed here some six or seven years ago the manufacturer must stamp upon every package the analysis, and the farmer is sufficient of a chemist to know the grade of mixture required for the different crops. I am not going to labour the point, but I only say again that I have tried to show the minister the enormous importance of this question of fertilizers to my own constituency. I am prepared to narrow it down to that, but what is true of my constituency is true of many other parts of New Brunswick. I am satisfied that the entire reduction in this duty would save my farmers $40,000 a year, and would not hurt the manufacturers of fertilizers at all, for a large portion of their output is being sold to the United States at $3 or $4 a ton less than it is sold for to our farmers.
Mr. A. IC. MACLEAN: Would the minister tell us what loss of revenue he anticipates from adding bananas to the exempted articles?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am unable to say offhand, but I do not think it is a very considerable amount.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is a large importation of bananas.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But on that importation the tax would not produce a very considerable

amount of revenue. The representations made to us by the government of Jamaica were of such a character that we thought we should have regard to them. The tax of 7i per cent would amount to about three or four cents a bunch of, say, eight dozen bananas. There is a feature of "it that is worthy of consideration, but was not the determinating factor with us, and that is that the business is conducted upon a pretty narrow margin of profit from the importer through the wholesaler to the vendor. The [DOT] revenue, in my judgment, was not sufficiently large to have induced us to change except upon the representations made.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My information is that the loss of revenue through this remission of duty will be very large.
I do not object to the change; on the contrary, I think it is a wise move not to collect a duty on bananas. They have become an important article of food, especially in the summer time, and on the part of the poorer class. If the figures which I have in my hands are correct the loss of revenue by putting them on the free list would be $2,000,000. That is the statement in the memorial furnished me by fruit importers:
It is estimated by those responsible for the tax that it would give the Government possibly $2,000,000 annually in revenue. These figures are based on the 44,000,000 bunches of bananas imported last year.
However, we all agree that the tax should be removed, and I have nothing more to say on the point. But I would like to take up, one by one, the different items the hon. gentleman has brought up, so that I may understand exactly where we are in this respect. We are all familiar with the resolutions brought down by my hon. friend; we have had them before us for five weeks. But to-day he has brought m a list of changes. The first of these is wild edible berries when imported from Newfoundland. I do not know whether it is worth while to discuss this matter, but I should like to know what that means. Berries are an article of diet, and it would be for the benefit of the consumer to have them admitted free. The use of fresh fruit is so important that I am sure no one will raise objection to this change. The minister stated that these were partridge berries. Are these the only berries that would come from Newfoundland? And can he tell us what the partridge berry is? In my province we know as partridge berry a small berry that grows in a bunch on a plant found in the forest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that the Scandinavians in Winnipeg are very desirous of getting these berries. I would not have introduced the amendment but that we were requested to make it by the government of Newfoundland, and it seemed a gracious thing to do. I would say that instead of the $2,000,000 being the expected revenue on bananas, had the change not been made, it would have been $200,000. Of course, I have no doubt that the right hon. gentleman has correctly read the memorial, but there is an error in the figures.

I think that the partridge berries referred to are known in other places as the fox berry. They are similar to the Nova Scotia cranberries, but have a flavour of their own. Considerable quantities of them are imported into Halifax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The next article is silk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Woven labels manufactured in silk come within the terms of the French treaty, and so it was not open to us to impose the duty of 7* per cent and 5 per cent upon these labels. But the war taxation as we proposed it applied to silk in the gum and spun silk. Therefore, had I not made these changes, the Canadian manufacturer of woven silk labels would have been called upon to pay a duty upon his raw material without any compensating duty upon the finished product entering into competition with him from France. So we have placed silk in the gum and spun silk imported for this manufacture in the list of exemptions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am not objecting, but I should like to know where that will lead us. The only article of the French treaty relating to silk is the last article in schedule (c) " manufactures of silk or of which silk is a component part."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would not cover this point, my hon. friend will observe.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
