speechtext: Exactly, but my hon. friend exempts only silk in the gum, because, he says, it comes under the provisions of the French treaty. Are not all articles of silk affected by the French treaty? Under the proposed tariff all articles of silk will be taxed 7J per cent; therefore the question arises as to whether or not we can increase duties upon articles which are mentioned in the French treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Some articles of silk, such as sewing and embroidery silk and silk underwear, do not come under the provisions of the French treaty. I understand that silk in the gum and spun silk are the only articles of silk which we need to exempt, for the reasons which I have given. Woven labels manufactured of silk come under the provisions of the French treaty; therefore, unless I place in the list of exemptions raw materials used by the Canadian manufacturer in making these silk products, he would be at a disadvantage compared with the position which he occupied before I brought down these changes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do I understand that all articles of silk which are mentioned in the French treaty shall not be subject to the new tariff of 7J per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All articles enumerated in schedule C of the French treaty are exempt from the operations of the 7J and the 5 per cent tariff. The duties in schedule C are specific and it is not open to us to alter them. I said in my Budget speech that I had regard to the convention with France and to our West India agreements in the proposals which I made.
Upon what principle is coffee taxed and tea exempt? Is there any scientific or plausible reason for the distinction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Coffee is, no doubt, used
generally, but I think that tea is in more general use among the poorer classes of the community than coffee is. In the West more coffee is consumed per head than in the East; of course they consume both tea and coffee. But what we had in view was that tea is, so to speak, the poor man's drink and we were reluctant to impose a duty upon it unless it was absolutely necessary to do so. So far as the present taxa-

speechtext: Has the Finance Minister classified in any way the revenue which he expects to get from the customs amendments? I should like to have a rough idea of the amounts he expects to get under the different headings.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only deal with that in a general way. Upon the returns for the fiscal year 1914, the taxation at 5 and 7J per cent, after making allowances for the exceptions, would run to something over $30,000,000.
That is the whole thing, special taxation and customs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, $30,000,000 for the taxation of 5 and 71 per cent customs; but as the revenues have fallen off, owing to the war and other causes, we have made a deduction from that amount, and, speaking from recollection, my estimate in the Budget speech was that we should raise from $20,000,000 to $25,000,000 from the imposition of the general taxation by customs duties. That would necessarily be subject to this; that it is not possible for me or any one else to foresee what the war may bring forth in the way of interruptions Of trade, trans-Atlantic or trans-Pacific trade; and in giving that estimate I qualified it, as I did my August estimate, by saying that I naturally submitted it with a great deal of diffidence, because it was not possible to forecast what the future would bring forth.
That is, you estimate it in the gross upon the increased ad valorem duties based upon the bulk of importations for the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I should like to
ask the minister why more exceptions have not been made in the line of agricultural implements. The only exceptions are reapers, mowers and binders. As far as those items are concerned, the minister knows and the Trade and Navigation returns show that there is very little importation in any event, and if the 7J per cent duty were added the importation -would cease. There is no doubt about that. It seems to me that there is very good reason why the 71 per cent is not added to reapers,

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Did the hon. gentleman say that there was an increase in the valuation?
I have been so informed on the very best authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I say there has been no increase in the valuation.

I must accept the minister's word, but I have been informed by implement dealers in western Canada who import these goods that the valuation of the ordinary eight-foot binder has since March 31, 1914, been increased by $22.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
That is not in accordance
with the facts. Perhaps my hon. friend is referring to the case of Hutchinson, who was given an interview to some of the papers.

I am not referring to newspaper interviews at all. The information comes to me from implement dealers in the city of Regina. If the minister assures me that there has been no increase in the valuation, I must accept his statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The International Harvester Company and all the other implement manufacturers on the other side of the line submit their price-lists to the Department of Customs each year, and it is on that valuation that the customs duties are collected. The hon. member will find that an answer was given in Hansard a few days ago showing there has been no increase in any shape or form in the valuation of agricultural implements, except in the case of Hutchinson, of the John Deere Plow Company. This company was importing binders into Canada at a valuation less than the home market price in the United States. Our appraiser learned of this and brought it to the attention of the department. The valuation was made equal to the home market prices in the United States, and that did not increase the price to the farmers of

Canada, for this reason: the John Deere Company's selling price in this country is just the same as that of the International Harvester Company and of other companies. The only thing is that before we made this change the John Deere Plow Company were making a much greater profit out of their binders by having them valued at $20 to $22 less than what they should have been. I know of no other case.
Has the valuation of the John Deere Plow Company's binder been increased?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: The price of the John Deere Plow Company's binder has been placed on the home market basis in the United States just the same as that of the International Harvester Company and other concerns. That is in accordance with the statute. The John Deere Plow Company were entering their binder at a price based on the cost of production at the factory.
At the cost price?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: At the cost price. The International Harvester Company were paying duty on the selling price on the other side of the line, whereas the John Deere Plow Company were getting their implements in at cost price and they were making a very much larger profit than the International Harvester Company who were paying the duty on the home market price. That is the only case I know of where the valuation was raised, but it was on account of these parties undervaluing their implements contrary to the provisions of the Customs Act. If the hon. gentleman has any other case to bring to my attention I will be very glad to explain it or find out if there is any reason why he should make such a statement.
I would like to find out from the minister if the basis of valuation on agricultural implements, and, I suppose other things, is the selling price in the country of production.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman reads the Customs Act he will see that it provides that the valuation for customs duties shall be the price for home consumption. We get the home consumption price- from the price list that is issued to the trade throughout the country from which the goods are being exported to Canada. In the case of agricultural implements, the International Harvester Company and others have their printed price lists which they submit to

the trade and it is on that basis that we must, under the law, collect the duty.

I have seen some of the price lists of the implement companies and in them are set forth the price that they charge what you might call the jobber and also the retail price at which the jobber sells to the' consumer. Is the price on which the duty is collected at the boundary the list price at which the company sells to the jobber or the price at which the jobber sells to the farmer in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The duty is collected on the
wholesale price as set forth in the price list, say, of the International Harvester Company. That is if they are selling to a concern in Canada. Suppose they were selling a carload of binders to a firm in Regina, they would invoice that carload at these prices and we would collect the duty on them. If they were to sell a carload to some concern in the United States and that firm retailed them out, the duty would be collected on the price at which the last sale was made if there was one binder brought in. If any person at Regina or any other place in the West were to buy from the International Harvester Company at the wholesale price wherever the goods are manufactured that would be the valuation upon which duty would be collected by the Customs Department.

Then the situation is just about wh t I thought it was. The duty is charged on the invoice price to the importer in western Canada. That being the provision I can readily understand how the difference in rue price of implements exists in the province of Saskatchewan as compared with the price in the states immediately south of that province. The same situation occurs in Manitoba and Alberta. I had a good opportunity last summer to investigate the question of the relative price of implements in the southern part of Saskatchewan, or in any part of Saskatchewan, and in the- states of the American Union bordering on Canada. From the information I got last summer, this information being in the form of sworn evidence given before a commission, I know it to be absolutely the case, and I do not think there is a single exception to what I say, that the prices of implements, wagons and all kinds of things used by the farmers in the province of Saskatchewan are from 15 to 20 per cent higher than they are in the states of North 74*
Dakota, Minnesota and other states immediately adjoining Canada. I remember last year reading in Hansard-I was not here when the debate occurred-

Does my hon.
friend refer to binders as well?
Binders as well.
My hon. friend is mistaken.

I have evidence on the
question. Last summer farmers came before the Implement Commission appointed by the Saskatchewn Government and gave evidence to the effect that the prices that they had paid for 8-foot and 6-foot binders in the states from which they had come and evidence of the prices which they had paid for International Harvesters, John Deere and Massey-Harris binders in the province of Saskatchewan. That evidence was given before a commission appointed by the Government of Saskatchewan for the purpose of investigating certain things in connection with the sale of agricultural implements. It is true that, the question of price was not the question: that was primarily brought before the commission but in almost every case, particularly in southern Saskatchewan, where a farmer came before that commission his first statement, particularly if he were a man who had come from the United States, was that the price of implements was far higher in Saskatchewan than it had been in the states bordering upon Canada. From the province of Ontario farmers gave evidence in regard to the comparative prices in Ontario and Saskatchewan, the prices in Saskatchewan being higher. That may be perfectly justifiable from the manufacturers' standpoint because we must pay freight on these binders, or whatever the machinery may be, from the point of manufacture in Ontario to the point of delivery in Western Canada and there must be some difference in price there. It is absolutely beyond doubt that there is a remarkable difference between the prices of implements in Saskatchewan and in the states to the south of the boundary line. My hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe) knows that that is the (case in respect to the province of Manitoba. It is absolutely true that the prices of implements in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta are, without any exceptions that I know of, higher by from 15 to 20 per cent than the same implements sell for in the states of the American Union immediately adjoining Canada.
I do not know anything of the kind. I know that the prices in North Dakota are very little less than they are in Manitoba.
They are a little less?
They are a little lessnot 5 per cent.

That is the only case
that my hon. friend can mention where the price comes anywhere near approximating the price charged in Manitoba. These articles come to mind in connection with the tariff on agricultural implements. We had this afternoon a statement from the Minister of Finance in respect to fertilizers. In Saskatchewan and in the other western provinces we do not use fertilizer to any great extent. At the same time, fertilizer is a very important thing to farmers in certain portions of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and agricultural implements, as far as the provinces of Saskatchewan and the other western provinces are concerned, are just as important to the farmers there as fertilizers are to the farmers of eastern Canada. If the Minister of Finance is justified in taking the duty off fertilizers for the benefit of the farmers of eastern Canada, why is he not justified in allowing the tariff to remain as it is at present on agricultural implements for the benefit of the farmers of western Canada? The patriotism and production campaign has been conducted chiefly in western Canada. There has been more talk about it in western Canada in so far as the production of wheat is concerned than in any other part of the Dominion. In western Canada, no matter whether we live in cities or towns, or in the country, we know that we are absolutely dependent for our success in the future on the success of the farming population.
We have not at the present time many manufacturing institutions in Regina, but the time may come when we shall, and I have no doubt the people of western Canada would be willing to extend to them a certain amount of consideration in the way of tariff. It appears to me that the Minister of Finance is not treating the farmers of western Canada fairly when he increases the duty on agricultural implements 7J per cent. This is a case where, in my opinion, exception might very well be made, as was made in the case of fertilizers. Excluding mowers, reapers, and binders, which pay a duty of 121 per cent, I find from the Trade and Navigation re-
[Mr. W. M. Martin. 1
turns that on the implements imported into Canada last year the duties ranged from 171 per cent to as high as 29-17 per cent.
Were many mow'ers, reapers, and binders imported into Canada last year ?

The number of mowers imported was small. Of reapers during the year 1913-14, only $38,000 worth was imported, and the duty paid was $6,702 or 171 per cent. There was imported $.336,675 worth of binders, on which the duty paid was $58,918 or 171 per cent. But on a large number of agricultural implements, which are used pretty nearly as much as mowers, reapers and binders, the duty paid ranged from 171 per cent to 29-17 per cent. If you add 71 per cent to this you will have a duty ranging from 25 per cent to 321 per cent, which i>s a fairly large tax on implements that are used by every farmer. In the case of a number of these implements there is practically no importation, so that the Minister of Finance will have no results if he has increased the duty on them for the purpose of raising revenue. I have never had very much objection to a tariff imposed from the standpoint of raising a revenue. It has been stated throughout this debate that the Liberal party has always stood for free trade; you will find free traders in the Liberal party, and in western Canada you will find free traders in the Conservative party. Some hon. members	on the	other	side
have accused me of attempting to raise issues between the East and the West, but I declare	here that
I have never adopted such a course. I have on several occasions stated that I believe in a tariff for revenue purposes, but that I did not believe in imposing a tariff from the standpoint of protection. I believe that the present tariff on agricultural implements, with this increase of 71 per cent, is a protective tariff. I also stated in this House some years ago that the proper way to frame a tariff was to pick out a large number of the items consumed by every man, woman and child in this country, put them on the free list, and then tax the luxuries. Under this rule agricultural implements would be placed on the free list. I have no objection to the Minister of Finance taxing automobiles as high as he wants to, and the duty on automobiles under this tariff will be 42 j per cent. If a man can afford to pay $2,500 for an automobile, he can pay a few hundred dollars more in duty or he should not want the

machine. I submit to the Minister of Finance that to do as he has done, namely, to take every article consumed by the farmers and by the labouring people, or used in their daily avocations, and to place an increase of 7) per cent duty on these articles, is not a scientific way to create a tariff. It certainly is not done with a view to placing the burden where it belongs; it is putting the burden on the agriculturist and on the working man who are least able to bear it. As I have said, there are a large number of agricultural implements which at the present time are not imported because of the high tariff, and to place an extra tariff of 71 per cent on them will certainly not bring in any revenue. I appeal to the Minister of Finance to leave the tax on agricultural implements as it was before this new tariff was brought down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member for Regina (Mr. W. M. Martin) that it is undesirable that we should discuss at this stage and at this time the general question of the duty upon agricultural implements. While it is probably true that fertilizers are not of much importance in the prairie provinces, yet they may become so in the future. My hon. friend will admit that mowing machines, harvesters, selfbinders and reapers are of probably more importance to the West than to the other sections of Canada, but he has overlooked the fact that in imposing an increase to the general and British preferential tariff upon practically the whole range of goods covered by our fiscal legislation, we have allowed reapers, and binders, and harvesters to remain at the rate of 121 per cent, to which they were reduced by this Government last year, the previous rate of duty having been 174 Per cent. I have on former occasions dealt with this question of the duty on agricultural implements quite frankly, and if my hon. friend will look at my remarks on the subject during the last regular session of this House, he will have my views. I looked into the question very carefully at the time, and I set forth my opinion with regard to the propriety of the tariff upon the facts of the investigations which I had made. My. lion, friend knows that there is a general drawback in respect of duties paid by manufacturers upon exported goods, and that with regard to reapers, binders and mowers there is in addition to that a drawback upon duties paid upon articles which are manufactured for domestic use in Canada. Therefore, this year, by reason of preserving that drawback I was enabled to leave the
duty on harvesters, reapers, binders and mowers at 124 per cent to which it had been reduced last year. As to the other range of agricultural implements to which the hon. gentleman calls attention, he is no doubt aware that there is no drawback to their manufacturers in respect of the duty they pay on raw material entering into their production in so far as the goods are sold in Canada. I pointed out in the course of the Budget debate that in approaching this question of raising additional revenue it became necessary for me to tax free goods and raw materials in order to increase our revenue. It is true, as my hon. friend has said, there are certain items in the tariff' upon which with the increase of duties we are not likely to get increases in revenue.
I calculate that, by reason of our imposing a duty upon free goods and raw materials, and also upon the finished article we shall add substantially to our revenues for the year.
Now, it follows from what I have said that, with the increase of duty upon iron, steel, lumber and other articles entering into the manufacture of the agricultural implements to which I now particularly refer, it will be obvious to my hon. friend who is acquainted with the principle of the adjustments we have to make in connection with the tariff, that the duty will have to be increased on the finished product. That was recognized by my predecessor whom I quoted last year, and it was my predecessor who gave the drawback to manufacturers on harvesters, reapers, binders and mowers of duties which they had paid on raw material entering into the products which they manufactured for home consumption. I think the differentiation between the two classes of agricultural implements will be obvious to my hon. friend. Where I was duties which they had paid on raw material not having been increased by these tariff proposals, I allowed the tariff to remain as it was. With regard to the other range of agricultural implements to which he has referred it will be obvious to him that it was necessary to increase the duties upon them by reason of the fact that we are increasing the duties on iron, steel, wood and other raw material that enter into the manufacture for home consumption. Among the-largest imports into Canada have been, those in the iron and steel schedules; and therefore it might be expected that we should derive a very substantial revenue from the imposition of these duties of 71

per cent and 5 per cent upon articles embraced in that category.
I think I have dealt sufficiently with what my hon. friend has drawn to our attention. I desire only to add that while we have left reapers, binders, mowers and harvesters at 12i per cent, we have kept binder twine on the free list as before, and also ditching-machines, of which there is no manufacture in Canada.

I should like to have made some observations on this subject before the minister replied to the hon. member for Regina (Mr. W. M. Martin). I endorse everything that was said by the hon. member for Regina, and would also point out to the Minister of Finance something which, perhaps, has already been *called to his attention. This question of agricultural implements is discussed wholly from the standpoint of the western farmer. But there are other classes relatively as important. They do not produce as much for export as the western farmer, but they do produce and support their families on their farms. There is just as large a population in eastern Canada supported by agriculture as in western Canada. In my own province, whose inhabitants are altogether an agricultural people, we find ourselves much hampered by this tariff. I can understand the argument of the Minister of Finance that in the case of all the agricultural implements other than those on which the tariff was reduced last year, the manufacturer has to pay duty on the raw material. Therefore, argues the hon. gentleman, the manufacturer should have a greater protection upon the finished product. I am not going to quarrel with that. But I am afraid that the minister has unduly magnified the amount which the manufacturer must pay on his raw material in order to bolster up his case for claiming the right to charge the consumer in eastern Canada the enormous prices he does. In my own province, as I have mentioned both yesterday and to-day, the great article of agriculture is potatoes. It may be that our people are wrong from an economic standpoint in going so heavily into the cultivation of potatoes. But they are doing it, and it is not within the power of myself or the Minister of Finance to interfere. They have thought the matter out, and they feel that they can make a better revenue with potatoes than with anything else.
'Mr. W. T. White.]
Now, they carry on this business in the maritime provinces on a large-scale. They have to have machines for this work. It may surprise the Minister of Finance to know how much the ordinary farmer in my constituency invests in these machines. He must have a reaper and in many cases a binder, though I realize that they are not nearly so important as in the West and also that in the East they buy a smaller machine. In addition they must have machinery to carry on their potato business and in this machinery they must invest from $300 to $400 and in some cases as much as $500. They must have, in the first place, a planter. The seed is placed in the hopper on this machine, and the machine makes the track, places the fertilizer, plants the potato and covers it up. You could never plant twenty acres of potatoes in the manner in which the Minister of Finance planted them when a boy-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I planted many of
them in that way.

Not to the extent of
twenty acres.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Certain modifications have been introduced in the resolution of which I gave notice, relating to the special taxation referred to in the Budget. They are as follows:
Purely mutual insurance companies are exempted from the tax of X per cent upon net premiums. There are agricultural insurance companies of a purely mutual character; we are exempting them from the special taxation.
Mutual fire insurance companies ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Purely mutual fire insurance companies.
Press despatches are exempted from the one-cent charge payable on messages sent by cable and telegraph companies'.
Steamship tickets on Atlantic seaboard. The one per cent charge on the cost of such tickets is enlarged to include all^ the West India islands instead of the British colonies in the West Indies, as stated in the resolution of which I gave notice. British Honduras has also been added.
Ocean passenger tickets. By the resolutions referred to in the Budget, an ocean passenger ticket costing $30 was subject to a tax of $3. By the new resolution the $30 has been increased to $40. By the first resolution an ocean ticket costing $60 was subject to a tax of $5. The $60 has been increased by the new resolution to $65. I shall explain the reason for that later on.
Promissory notes. Promissory notes, dis-. counted or sent for collection through a bank, are made subject by the new resolution to the stamp tax of two cents. Promissory notes were not made subject to the new tax along with cheques and bills of exchange by the first resolution.
Patent medicines and perfumery. The stamp tax of one cent on each 10 cents of retail value has been changed in the new resolutions to one cent on each 25 cents worth of retail value, a reduction from 10 per cent to 4 per cent.	-
Wines, non sparkling. By the first resolution, each one quart or less was subject to five cents stamp tax. That is changed by the new resolution so that a pint or less should have a stamp of only three cents.
Champagne. By the first resolution, each pint or less was to bear a stamp tax of 25 cents. That is changed so that a half pint or less shall pay only 13 cents. There are half pints of champagne which are not especially referred to in the first resolutions.
These are the changes which are embodied in the new resolutions which I shall now hand to the chairman.
By which section is the promissory note added as being taxable, section 8?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When I had under consideration the resolutions relating to the stamp tax on bills of exchange. I considered also the question of imposing a stamp tax on promissory notes. It occurred to me at the time it would be undesirable that that should be done because promissory notes are very common instruments passing between individuals in all parts of the Dominion, and it would be difficult to institute a system of taxation on such promissory notes. We therefore determined that we would limit the taxation of two cents imposed by stamp tax to bills of exchange negotiated through a bank and to cheques. It has been pointed out to us, and we recognized the force of the statements made, that the Act could be evaded so far as it related to bills of exchange negotiated through banks unless the taxation were also imposed upon promissory notes negotiated at or through banks.
This would be an increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and if desired I can let this stand as a notice of motion until to-morrow.
Will the man who makes out the cheque have to put on the stamp or the bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The maker of the cheque is obliged to put it on, but if he does not the duty is imposed on the bank of seeing that it is put on.
A special stamp will be provided for the purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Do I understand that a note passing between individuals which, does not go through a bank does not need to have the stamp on it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, we have omitted those.
And bills of exchange the same way?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Bills of exchange between individuals, but to bills of exchange negotiated through a bank the stamp applies.

The minister has announced some changes in the resolution. Would he be good enough to explain why life and marine insurance companies were excepted? Clause 3 provides that every insurance company other than life and marine companies and fraternal benefit societies shall pay a tax. I could understand why fraternal benefit societies might very well be excepted, but why life and marine companies should be exempted and fire insurance companies be obliged 9 p.m. to pay, I am not quite able to understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I had a much larger range of companies under consideration for special taxation than appeared in the resolutions now before the Committee. I considered very carefully the question of imposing a tax on life insurance companies, and discussed it with our Insurance Department very fully. My hon. friend is aware that there are fraternal benefit societies, and it did not appear desirable that they should be taxed because the taxation would fall upon their policy-holders. That is also true in the case of the life insurance companies carrying on an ordinary business, because there is a division of profit. My hon. friend knows that there are charges loaded upon the policies. And then there are mutual life insurance companies. It did not appear to me, giving the matter the best consideration of which I was capable, that it would be advisable that this tax-
ation should fall in any substantial measures upon the policy-holders of life insurance companies, because life insurance is a matter of such extreme importance to the individual and to his family. It seemed to me that we might very properly differentiate in our taxation in favour of the policy-holders of life insurance companies. The Superintendent of Insurance reports without any hesitation that any taxation that might be imposed upon life insurance will be borne by the policyholder, and it is his view, and it is mine, that the policy-holders of the companies should not be burdened with taxation in making provision for 'their dependents.
Whether those are good reasons it is for the committee to judge. But it appeared to me that, having regard to these and some other considerations that are obvious and anala-gous to those I have mentioned, it would be advisable to exempt life insurance companies from this taxation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Does not that apply to all these taxes?
Mr. W'HITE: Not in the same degree, I think. Legislation has specially recognized that life insurance policies are a class of property different from other property. For example, under provincial legislation, and I think Dominion, it is possible for one to declare a trust or to make a policy payable without consideration to a dependent or to his family, and the law will not set that aside at the instance of any creditor. So that life insurance policies have been regarded as a class of property different from other property; I think for the reason of the dependence of a man's family upon his life insurailce policy. Whether that appeals to the committee or not it is for them to say. But, in the opinion of the Superintendent of Insurance, these taxes will fall on the policy-holders and upon a man's dependents, and as all classes of the community are interested in life insurance, we thought it inadvisable to impose this tax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is a great deal of force in the views presented by my hon. friend. If there is a class of property that ought to be sacred, it is certainly an insurance policy. An insurance policy is a sort of a trust. For instance, a young man going into business sets aside a certain portion of his earnings every year for the possible contingency that the insurance may be paid to his family. There is no more sacred trust, and I should be sorry for us to do anything here to impair the

value of that trust. But, take the ordinary stock companies, not the mutual companies. Take the Canada Life, for instance, or the Sun Life and other companies that earn a very large income. I do not know what rate of dividend they pay to their shareholders, but I imagine it must be pretty high. Is it not possible that the profits which are accumulated and go to the shareholders might just as well be subject to taxation as the profits of the banks or trust companies, or of any other dividend earning company?
I can see no reason at present why this should not apply to insurance companies.

With the view that, has just been expressed by the right hon. gentleman I entirely agree. I had occasion to look into that matter the other day and, while the profits of life insurance companies arise from several sources, I think the nonprofit bearing policies should probably not be subject to this tax; for a non-profit bearing policy is merely a contract between the insurance company and the insured by which for a definite premium the company undertakes to pay under 'certain contingencies a fixed sum. But with policies that earn so-called profits the company not only accumulates large sums of money by reason of the loading of the premiums based upon the expectation of life tables, but it also makes large sums of money from the investment of its surplus funds, and while in theory some portion of its surplus funds belongs to the policy-holders and is distributed sometimes annually, sometimes quinquennially, and sometimes at other intervals, nevertheless the owners of the company are in complete control and dominate those profits; and there is no reason why they should not pay something to the revenue of this country at this time, just as much as something should be contributed from the accumulated profits of banks or trust companies. I think the" tax should certainly apply to joint stock companies such as the Sun Life, the Canada Life, the Confederation Life and the Great West, which have a paid up capital stock and an accumulated surplus representing in some instances many times what their paid up capital stock is.
There is another matter to be kept in mind, and which perhaps may militate somewhat against the views I have expressed, and perhaps the Minister of Finance had this in mind. I refer to the enormous taxes that have been imposed on these companies by the provinces. It was only yesterday I think that Mr. Justice
Middleton gave his decision that the taxes in Ontario were intra vires. It had been alleged that it was a direct tax which could not be enforced by the province. That was one of the grounds, and I need not discuss the others, but it was held competent for the province to pass that legislation. And that involves the consideration up to what point this taxation can be carried without necessitating a revision of the contracts that exist between the companies and the policy-holders. I think that is well worthy of the consideration of the Finance Minister before we finally settle this matter. The shares of some of these large life insurance companies are selling on the market at $300, and in one instance the price was $321 for a hundred dollar share.

I am not able to see why these life insurance companies should not pay a contribution to the treasury under the present circumstances. It must be borne in mind that the tax, alleged to be a war tax, ds imposed under circumstances which the Finance Minister thinks justify the imposition of this burden, and the allegation is made that it is placed on all the people of Canada so that each one may contribute something towards the revenue. Take the case of fire insurance companies. They can change their rates every year, and I venture to say that if this tax is continued for any length of time they will take it out of their policy-holders by a little increase in the premiums. They know how to do that. The banks know how to take it out of their customers. If they are obliged to pay a tax they add a percentage to the rate of interest which they charge. In the end the bulk of these taxes will come out of the people who transact business with these large financial institutions. Life insurance companies doing business in Canada give evidence that they are making a great deal more money than fire insurance companies. On the whole, fire insurance in Canada has not been a profitable business for some years past; but life insurance has on the whole been exceedingly profitable.
Mr. R. B. BENNETT. Most profitable.

Go to the great cities of Canada, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Hamilton or Vancouver, and you will find great buildings towering to the sky almost, owned by life insurance companies; magnificent buildings used not only by the life insurance companies themselves, but rented out for office purposes, from which they derive a large revenue. The business

done by life insurance companies in Canada is enormous. I have the figures for 1913 showing that the net amount of life insurance in force in Canada was $1,168,590,027. Of that the insurance carried by Canadian companies was $750,637,902; by British and Colonial companies, $58,176,795; and the balance by United States companies doing business in Canada, and remember that would include such great companies as the Equitable, the Mutual Life, the New York Life, the Prudential and other companies whose assets are counted in hundreds of millions of dollars.
Yet under this Bill these great and wealthy companies are allowed to go scot free while the taxes are being imposed upon fire insurance companies. If the premium rate on fire insurance is increased it strikes most people just as hard as it would strike them if a small amount were taken away from the profits divided amongst the policy-holders of the life insurance companies.
It would not strike them any harder than it does in the case of fire insurance companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Do these figures include
the mutual companies?
They include the mutual companies as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Companies like the Independent Order of Foresters?
AH. PUGSLEY: Yes.
Not the Foresters.

They do not include
benevolent societies.
I presume that is so.
They include all companies that come under the Insurance Act.

The tax proposed is one per cent on the net premiums received.
If a tax were imposed upon premiums ag-[Mr. Pugsle'-1
gregating $38,641,206 it would give about $380,000 of additional revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that that would include the Independent Order of Foresters?

I presume it would, but I assume that insurance carried by the fraternal companies would be only a small percentage. Take the fire companies; the fire policies in force in 1913 aggregate $2,925,200,553 and the premium paid thereon $35,347,139. The premiums received by the life insurance companies in 1913 were about $3,000,000 greater than the premiums collected by fire insurance companies. It does seem to me that all companies, with the exception of what may be termed purely mutual fraternal companies, ought to be subjected to this tax. If you are going to provide a tax that is to bear as far as possible upon all classes in the community, there is no possible justification for taxing fire insurance companies and exempting life insurance companies, which are, speaking in a general way much more wealthy and much more able to pay the tax than fire insurance companies are.

With reference to the
level premiums I would like to say non-participating policies are loaded in their charges for the purpose of providing dividends for the stockholders just as much as the participating polices. The hon. member for Calgary (Air. Bennett) is quite right in saying that the stockholders and directors have absolute control of the question as to the amount of profits that are going to the policy-holders and the amount they shall take for themselves. The non-participating policies are loaded for this purpose.
That is in order to pay the level premium as distinguished from the natural premium.

Yes. I would not like the committee to think that * there were many level premium mutual companies doing business in Canada. The benevolent societies are a different proposition. I did not rise to urge the imposition of a tax on life insurance companies, although I presume they could stand it, as my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) says, a good deal better than fire insurance companies. To my certain knowledge the large fire insurance companies have not made any money in this country for thirty years. I rose to direct the attention of my hon. friend the Alinister of Finance to the fact

that there is a large amount of fire insurance done in Canada by companies that do not pay a cent towards the maintenance of the Government in this country. They do business principally with the large corporations, and they pay no license fees. I have always contended that if we are going to license one we should license all and put all on the same basis. They are also exempt from this tax, notwithstanding the fact that they gather an enormous amount of insurance in this country. Last year they had insurance in force to the extent of $250,000,000. These companies are exempt, and I do not think it is fair that they should be exempt.
They are what are called mill mutuals?

Mill mutuals, reciprocal underwriters and various mutuals. They collect a cash premium in this country, and they are all Americans. They pay nothing. They are not corporations that pay liberally towards the upkeep of the country.
They do not even have an agent here.

No, they pay nothing to anybody in this country. The large fire insurance companies help to a large extent in maintaining our cities. They erect fine buildings, pay enormous taxes, and are the largest purchasers of gilt-edged securities. They have to have their moneys available in case of losses, and in consequence they invest only in gilt-edged securities. They are a very great asset to the country because of the excellent premises they have and the taxes they pay towards the maintenance of the different cities.
Air. AAT. F. AIACLEAN: We are discussing an emei'gency tax, but we have raised another question as to the profit of insurance companies. These profits are very large. They have a different way of dealing with these financial corporations ini Germany which is well worthy of consideration, not in connection with an emergency tax like this, but in connection with the question of what the insurance companies ought to contribute towards the revenue of the country. The large life insurance companies make enormous profits, and, instead of sharing these profits fairly with the policy-holders, they hand them over largely to the shareholders. In Germany they make large insurance companies, banks and other corporations of this class share their profits, first, with the state, and, iri the next place, they compel them to apply excess profits to a reduction in the rates.
Eventually we will have to come to that in this country, both as regards banks and insurance companies. There is no reason why the insurance companies in Canada should not pay a percentage of their profits to the State, and be made to share their profits every year. It has been worked out in other countries, it can be worked out here. A large revenue would accrue to the State from that source, and no one can stand it so well as the shareholders who own these companies. They do not reduce rates when they could reduce rates, and they have these large profits which are ultimately held for the benefit of the shareholders. These profits should be divided with the State ox with the policy-holders, and our general insurance company law should be amended in that direction. We are taking an emergency tax from the banks on their circulation. Probably the best way to reach them in connection with a permanent form of taxation, would be to make the banks share their profits with the State, or increase the rate of interest to the depositors. My suggestion is that the Government should have in view a permanent policy in the direction I have indicated. In the meantime I agree largely with what lias been said, that probably you could get a large revenue by putting some kind of an emergency tax on these profits right away.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a distinction between a bank and a life insurance company carrying on modern life insurance. If a bank makes certain profits as a result of its annual operations, it is open to the bank to distribute the entire sum of these profits among its shareholders, who are really the proprietors, or to carry a portion of the profits to reserve. In the case of a life insurance company, as distinct from a fire insurance company, a bank, or a general joint stock company, there is the relationship of partnership between the life insurance company and its policyholders; there is the relationship of trustee and cestui que trust except as to capital. Therefore, in my view, you should not deal with a life insurance company upon the same principle as you would deal with a bank or an institution in which that fiduciary relationship or partnership relationship does not exist, unless you are prepared to go this far:	that you are willing
to impose taxation not only upon the institution in so far as it is owned by its shareholders, but also upon the policy-

holders who are participators in its profits, who are charged with a share of the expenses, and who are, in a sense, partners in the business. It is true, as stated by my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley), that certain life insurance companies are very large and wealthy institutions, but it is equally true that there are also many life insurance companies, especially those organized during recent years-and this also would be true of fire insurance companies-which have paid no dividends to their shareholders.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are there any companies which have paid no dividends to their shareholders?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Assistant Deputy Minister tells me there are several. My starting point is that it is not desirable to tax fraternal life insurance companies, or to tax mutual life insurance companies, or to tax ordinary life insurance companies if the burden of taxation will inevitably be shifted upon the policy-holders. This matter has engaged my most careful attention and the superintendent of insurance, who is a skilled actuary and a man whose judgment *is' entitled to great weight, says:
It has been stated that since insurance contracts of life insurance companies are made with fixed and definite premiums throughout life, which cannot be increased, any additional tax imposed must be borne by the shareholders. It must be remembered, however, that 85 per cent of the life insurance in Canada is on the participating plan under which profits realized over and above claims and expenses are distributed amongst the policy-holders. Any tax imposed upon the premiums of life insurance companies would be immediately treated as an additional expense on the business, and would, therefore, go to reduce the profits payable to policy-holders, and, therefore, to increase the net cost of insurance to those policyholders. The tax would therefore be borne by the policy-holders as truly as if the premiums they pay were immediately increased by the amount of the tax.
Yes, but that could be changed. You could tax the net profits of the insurance companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They would treat that tax as part of their expenses and it would be loaded on the policy-holders.
But they have no right to put that load on the policy-holders.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The superintendent of insurance has been engaged in the inspection and examination of insurance for many years and he says that is precisely what would happen. He says further:

It is believed to be impossible to so tax life insurance companies as to make the burden fall upon the shareholders, but that it would in every case be transferred to the policy-holders of the company.

How could that be so? Take the Canada Life Insurance Company and it is provided by statute that its dividends shall not exceed ten per cent, that is $100,000 per annum on one million dollars. The accumulated surplus which arises from the profits on investment, as well as from the loading of the premiums, amounts . to a very large sum. Why should this not pay some tax to the state?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All I can do is to invoke the technical opinion of the man who is dealing with insurance companies every day.
Yes, under existing conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This gentleman says it would be loaded upon the policy-holders. In addition to that he says that no less than 85 per cent of the life insurance in Canada is on the participating plan.
How is that participation appropriated to policy-holders and to shareholders?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By the directors who, as a matter of fact, are given that statutory authority.
That is where the whole trouble is; they should not have that statutory authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the insurance law of this country to-day.

I know it, and it is
crying for reform.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That may be a question for consideration but I am speaking of the situation as it exists to-day and 85 per cent of life insurance is participating and in the opinion of the Dominion Superintendent of Insurance the burden of this taxation, if we imposed it, would fall upon the policyholders. Assuming, as I have assumed, that it is not wise that we should tax policy-holders of life insurance, in view of this expert opinion of the Insurance Department and of the legislation as it is to-day I was unable to see that I would be justified in imposing a tax upon life insurance companies, and that is the reason they were exempted.
My hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) raised another question, as to un-

licensed companies. I looked carefully into that matter. My hon. friend knows that these unlicensed companies have no offices in Canada and no agents here. As he has pointed out, they are not subject to the jurisdiction of the Dominion, not being domiciled here. This matter has already been considered by this House and by the Senate. The question of taxation of premiums paid to unlicensed insurance companies was the subject of a prolonged and heated argument before the Banking and Commerce Committee of the House of Commons in 1909 and before the Banking and Commerce Committee of the Senate in 1910, the parties being, on one side the Canadian Fire Underwriters' Association representing most of the licensed insurance companies, and on the other side representatives of many large manufacturing companies. The licensed insurance companies urged either the prohibition of this unlicensed insurance or the imposition of a tax on the premiums paid to these unlicensed companies equal to the percentage of the premiums the licensed companies were called upon to pay by reason of their compliance with the Canadian Insurance Act. The rate of taxation then advocated was 15 per cent. Against this contention it was urged that the right of contracting outside of Canada for insurance in unlicensed companies was one which should not be taken from the individual in Canada, nor should such transaction be subject to taxation. It was claimed also that the difference between the rates charged by the licensed companies and those charged by the unlicensed companies for the same class of risk was much greater than could be accounted for by the expense caused by compliance with the Insurance Act, and this large difference was not satisfactorily explained. I understand that no action was taken except this-that every person in Canada effecting insurance in an unlicensed company was required to make a return to the Department of Insurance showing the amount of such insurance placed by him during the calendar year.

My memory is that the
House of Commons passed the Senate amendment as it stands in section, 39.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was not a member of the House at that time and am not familiar with the facts. If the hon. gentleman says that that was the case I accept his statement.

I am speaking from
memory, but I was a member of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The net result was, after
the matter had been discussed in the Banking and Commerce Committee of both the House and the Senate, each individual insured in an unlicensed company was required to make the return to which I have referred.
Now, let us see whether it is possible, as my hon. friend suggests, that these companies should be covered by our special taxation measures. They are not domiciled in Canada, and I understand that the agent who arranges for the insurance is regarded as the agent of the insured and not of the insuring company. Therefore, the only way we could impose a tax would be to impose it upon the premiums paid by the individual-tax the individual instead of the company. That is a different principle from the principle which we are adopting under this Act. We are not taxing the individual who may insure with the insurance company. We are taxing the insurance companies one per cent on their net premiums. Precisely how that tax may be borne, I am unable to say. It may be absorbed in whole or in part by the company, but it is clear that the taxation is primarily against the company upon its net premium income. The other would be a tax direct against the individual, upon the premiums paid to these unlicensed companies. The two principles are not on all-fours. I speak not without a certain sympathy with the attitude of the fire insurance companies in this matter, because they are in competition with the unlicensed companies. My own view is that if the situation requires a remedy, it should be remedied in such a way that the unlicensed companies doing business here shall be brought under the jurisdiction of the Dominion Government in some way. Whether that will be done or not I am not prepared at the moment to say. But that is a matter which will engage my attention in connection with some subsequent revision of the Insurance Act. Giving the matter my best consideration for the present, I am unable to see how the provisions of this taxation measure can be made to apply to the unlicensed companies which have no offices in Canada, no agent and no domicile in Canada to bring them under the jurisdiction of the Dominion Government.

I quite agree with the Minister of Finance. The best way to get at it is through the Insurance Act. At the same time, I would point out to the

hon. minister that since the time of the controversy of which he speaks, the companies of the Underwriters' Association have put themselves in a position to write sprinklered risks at practically the same rates as the unlicensed companies, having established a sprinkler department since that time. I must say it is absolutely unfair in this country, where we allow a certain protection even under a revenue tariff, to force the licensed companies to help to keep, up the country while the unlicensed companies that have nothing at stake can come into the country and do a great deal of the gilt-edged business and pay nothing whatever towards the up-keep of the country. I think the minister could have got at this by taxing the premiums paid by the individual. Under clause 139 of the Insurance Act the individual has to report the amount of his unlicensed * insurance. He might as well report the amount of the premium paid at the same time. It would not be more difficult to compel him to report the amount of the premium paid than to compel him to report the amount of the insurance written.

Of course, a great deal might be said for the taxing of some long-established insurance companies; but I think on the whole it would work an injustice to the policy-holders if life insurance companies generally were included; and I think that the minister's decision to exclude them from the provision of that clause is, on the whole, wise. I rose to suggest that, as it is improbable that we can conclude the consideration of these amendments this evening, and as we sat to a very late hour this morning, and hon. members are more or less tired, we adjourn, and in all probability it will not take very long to dispose of the resolutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The suggestion of the hon. member is entirely agreeable to me. I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, to resume to-morrow.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and progress reported.
On motion of Mr. White, the House adjourned at 9.45 p.m.
Thursday, March 18, 1915.
